Centers and Institutes
8.90.10 The following sections, 8.90.10-8.90.40, establish the administrative procedures for Centers and Institutes at URI. Centers and Institutes are of two types: Academic and Institutional. This section of the University Manual deals with Academic Centers and Institutes. Institutional Centers and Institutes are considered in other parts of the University Manual and/or other University governing documents. Academic Centers and Institutes are officially recognized units that shall be established with the purpose of advancing scholarly, instructional, training, service, and/or outreach activity through collaborative research or creative endeavors. Notwithstanding any provision stated here or any arrangements derived from these sections, curricular matters shall always and only be reserved as the concern of departments, colleges, schools, and academic experiences, and the hiring and primary housing of academic staff shall be reserved for departments, colleges, and schools.

An Academic Center has a focused mission and a clearly defined objective to facilitate collaboration at the university. It may involve a group of faculty from one or more departments from a single college or school or from different colleges and schools. An Academic Center must have no fewer than three core faculty members (including the director). The governance of an Academic Center should generally not involve more than one college or school, but exceptions may be approved if a compelling case is made by the proposers at the time of application.
An Academic Institute has a broad but clearly defined mission to promote interdisciplinary collaboration within and beyond the University. Academic Institutes may bring together many disciplines, departments, colleges, schools, and other institutions to create local, national, and/or international partnerships.

The feasibility of a proposed Academic Center or Institute using the term “Center” or “Institute” will be supported by the proposal documents and ultimately determined by the Centers and Institutes Review Committee (CIRC), the Faculty Senate, and the final determination by the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs. Existing centers and institutes may retain their current designations as a center or an institute, with possible reevaluation of these definitional classifications at the time of renewal.
Each Academic Center or Institute is an individual entity and not tied to the demise or expansion of other Academic Centers or Institutes.
The list of active academic centers and institutes shall be maintained by the Office of the Provost and shared with the Division of Research and Economic Development, the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, and the Center and Institutes Review Committee. #11-12–25, #17-18-23 #20-21-32 #25-26-FSEC-08

8.90.25 Governance. A proposal for an Academic Center or Institute that includes more than one college or school in its activities and governance shall articulate the structure, membership, and function of a governing body of personnel drawn from among the participating units, and from external units/institutions in appropriate cases. The governing body shall be empowered to propose changes to the Academic Center or Institute’s charter, with support for the proposed changes indicated in letters from every participating unit. Proposals for change shall seek approval in turn by CIRC, the Faculty Senate, the Vice President for Research and Economic Development (for research centers and institutes), and the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs. In cases where a governing body cannot reach consensus on its own, the Provost shall mediate. No participating unit shall be prevented from departing from an Academic Center or Institute after notice to CIRC, the Faculty Senate, the Vice President for Research, and the Provost, and after suitable provision has been made to account for the departing unit’s existing obligations to the Academic Center or Institute. #25-26-FSEC-08

8.90.30 Review. Each Academic Center and Institute shall be reviewed every four years. The governing body articulated in the charter, or the director of an academic center housed in a single college or school, shall present to CIRC an application for review and renewal. All participating units and the Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall be solicited for comments, which must be included with the review. A reporting template for the review can be obtained from CIRC or the Faculty Senate Office. The review will be based on overall outcomes relevant to the Academic Center’s or Institute’s mission and goals (see section 8.90.20). CIRC should endeavor to include all information relating to the Academic Center or Institute in a report that shall form the foundation for further evaluation. The CIRC recommendation should state one of two options: renewal or probation. In the case of a recommendation of probation, the academic center or institute shall have one year to present an application for renewal, at which time CIRC will perform a new review; CIRC’s recommendation should be one of two options: renewal or dissolution. No dissolution shall occur except for a year of probation having intervened. CIRC, the Faculty Senate, the Vice President for Research, or the Provost may request a review outside the normal schedule. Immediate suspension or dissolution may occur in rare and severe circumstances.

The results of the review of academic centers and institutes will be included in CIRC’s annual report to the Faculty Senate. Recommendation to dissolve an academic center or institute can be initiated by its leadership for any reason; by CIRC or the Senate for reporting failures; and by the Provost or Vice President for Research and Economic Development for failure to meet stated goals.
The dissolution process will entail a CIRC review (as detailed above), notice to the Faculty Senate and (for research centers and institutes) the Vice President for Research and Economic Development, and a final determination by the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs. Dissolved centers and institutes will be removed from the list of active academic centers and institutes. Dissolved Academic Centers and Institutes shall remove webpages, materials, and signage from public view, and cease using the Academic Center’s or Institute’s name for internal or external activities or funding. Defunct websites shall be rendered read-only and placed in the University archives. #02-03-14 #09-10-16 #11-12-25, #17-18-23, #17-18-23, #20-21-32 #21-22-29 #25-26-FSEC-08

Honors contracts allow students to earn credit for non-Honors coursework by pursuing more advanced study by special agreement with the instructor and approval by the Honors Program. After considering several options, including a discussion at the Faculty Senate Meeting, the FSEC decided that one change in the election procedures might resolve some of the issues of concern.
The FSEC thinks that if the Faculty Senate Chair and Vice Chair were elected earlier in the spring semester (February rather than May) the new officers would have the opportunity to observe and become familiar with the major issues being considered by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, the Strategic Planning and Budget Council (SBPC) and the Joint Committee on Academic Planning (JCAP) and when they assume their offices in May there would be little or no interruption in continuity.

In addition, when Senators are asked to run for office they consult with their respective department chairs and deans about their schedule for the following academic year.
When this takes place in May, there is less opportunity for some Senators to run for office since commitments have already been made for the following year.
Also Senators and their departments must rush to figure out what can be done to compensate for the ½ and 1/3 reduction in load to which they are entitled.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee recommends that the Faculty Senate approve the following amendments to the Faculty Senate By-Laws to allow officer elections earlier in the spring semester.

These changes were approved in Bill #21-22-21B: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1XlqSOuKERd_Y6K0WFIExcj3piek-0k3z/view Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship - Specialty, Effective Summer 2025 Appendix B Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.

Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.
The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.

The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.

Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.

The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States.

The University mission situates the University as a land, sea, and urban grant institution serving Rhode Island and beyond, that is bound by the core values of creativity and scholarship; diversity, fairness, and respect; engaged learning and civic involvement; and intellectual and ethical leadership.
The Graduate Track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship will especially foster URI’s values of diversity, fairness and respect in students.
Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship supports URI’s mission by supporting diverse communities.
Additionally, the track will foster the leadership and critical thinking skills needed in a diversifying country and workforce.

Presently, MBA students can earn our Online Ocean Science Graduate Certificate and use these credits towards the MBA degree.
An in-person program will benefit the in-person Blue MBA program because there is a much larger number of in- person elective class offerings than there are online.
Taking online classes is cumbersome for in-person MBA students as URI Online requires separate tuition and is on a different academic calendar than the in-person calendar.
Effectively, the present situation requires students to disenroll from the in-person MBA program and enroll in the online certificate program to complete the Blue MBA program.
The present cumbersome situation was recognized as a problem in conversations between GSO and the College of Business and it was jointly agreed that GSO would propose an in-person certificate to streamline and enhance the Blue MBA program.
The URI Strategic Plan explicitly calls for an increase in graduate student enrollment and creating a diverse learning community which ensures that a URI education is within reasonable reach for all students.

This proposed certificate program will 1. make the Blue MBA more attractive to potential students and 2. increase the number of graduate students by creating a program for those who are not ready to commit to a master's degree program The program will be an expanded version of our online Ocean Science Graduate Certificate.
There are many more electives which can be taken in person than online.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION JANUARY 23, 2025 Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2024-2025-05B At the December 19, 2024 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate for approval. Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: BA Criminology & Criminal Justice, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix A CCJ seeks to add 3 new elective classes to its curriculum. CCJ 285 and CCJ 456 have been approved by the CCJ faculty as criminal justice elective options for majors and CCJ 334 has been approved as a criminology elective. CCJ 285 (Fac Sen Bill # 23-24-19) and 456 (Fac Sen Bill # 24-25-01) have been fully routed and approved through the curriculum process. CCJ 334 is currently being routed through the process (submitted for the October 14 A&S curriculum committee meeting) but we seek to include the class in this NOC of change to reduce the need for curriculum modifications moving forward as the department intends to offer this class as soon as the 25-26 AY. BFA Theatre, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix B Changes approved for addition of THE200 to the curriculum per Faculty Senate Bill # 22-23-39A passed and signed by President on 23.04.20. This course (THE200) replaces two previous courses: THE291 (2 cr) and THE391 (2 cr). It is intended to make the production courses less complicated and confusing for students, allowing for consistency of the numbering system.

COLLEGE OF EDUCATION: BS Health & Physical Education, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix C Curricular changes are intended to align with national norms and availability of university course offerings.
The changes will offer students flexibility to select professional electives that closely align with their unique career goals in health and physical education.
COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Geology & Geological Oceanography, Effective Fall 2025 Appendix D The current program has two options (Geology option and Geological Oceanography option).
We propose to add the Water and Climate Sciences as a third option.
The total number of credits in intro & professional courses, core geosciences and option specific courses, electives and supporting sciences is not changing, i.e. the number of credits will be comparable to the currently existing options.
However, option specific core course GEO 200, GEO 234 and GE0 280 replace GEO 210, GEO 320, GEO 370 and GEO 450.
Please refer to the advising sheet for the new Water and Climate Sciences option.
Copies of the existing (unchanged) advising sheet for the other two options are included for reference.

No new courses need to be created for the proposed changes.
Existing courses added to the revised core program are taught at a frequency that ensures degree completion in four years.
All existing classes have the capacity to accommodate additional inflow of students or, if needed, new class sections can be opened.
Students in the current options will not be affected by the proposed changes.
NEW SPECIALIZATIONS COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: Specialization in Water & Climate Science (BS Geology & Geological Oceanography), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix E The specialization in Water and Climate Sciences allows students the flexibility to define their own area of concentration within the water and climate sciences.
Example areas of concentration include environmental geology/ hydrogeology, and climate.
Students will be well prepared to pursue careers in environmental consulting, water resource management, sustainability initiatives, climate adaptation and resilience, and the emerging field of climate analytics.
These career opportunities are available with national and international government agencies, non-profit organizations, and the private sector.

The program will also equip students for research roles both in academia and the private sector.
Specialization Requirements: - All of the following courses: GEO200, GEO234G, GEO280, GEO305G, GEO483; GEO420 and/or GEO422; GEO482 and/or GEO484 - 24 credits of GEO courses at the 300-level or above

COLLEGE OF HEALTH SCIENCES: Specialization in Kinesiology (BS Kinesiology), Effective Fall 2025 Appendix F The Kinesiology Track provides flexibility to choose professional electives appropriate for a wide range of health and exercise science related careers. It is appropriate for students interested in pursuing health care professions such as physical therapy, chiropractic, medical doctor, or physician’s assistant or in becoming an exercise physiologist, strength and conditioning specialist, occupational therapist or health coach. Career opportunities exist in corporate, community, commercial and hospital-based fitness and wellness centers. The Kinesiology track will also prepare students for graduate study in clinical exercise physiology, cardiac rehabilitation, exercise science, health fitness, health promotion, preventive medicine and related fields. Kinesiology students will be prepared to become a certified professional in specialty areas including exercise physiology, strength and conditioning and/or personal training. The Kinesiology Track requirements include: 1. One of: PSY 200, STA 220, 307, or 308 2. 12 credits from the list of professional electives, with a minimum of 6 credits from KIN courses: CHM 105, 124, 126; CMB 210; EDC/HLT 401; KIN 125, 243, 369, 375G, 414, 425, 464G, 482; NUT 360; PSY 255. Other KIN or health-related courses may apply with approval from the KIN Department Chair. Additionally, there are free electives. Any student interested in graduate education should check programs of interest for prerequisites. Free electives can be used to satisfy those prerequisites.
